editorNote: The week's sharpest security story is architectural, not adversarial: researchers found that Anthropic, OpenAI and Google were all encrypting chain-of-thought with the same key across a model family, letting anyone replay a frontier model's hidden reasoning through a weaker sibling and read it in plaintext — since patched. OpenAI shipped the inverse of caution, an 'offense-grade' hacking model gated behind vetted access, while its own ethics chief quit within a year of joining. London's transit police pushed live facial recognition onto the Underground, and a medical-research vendor's 'never AI' pitch turned out to be almost entirely AI. One blog post ties it all together: compression and prediction were always the same problem.

stories.headline: Researchers extract hidden reasoning from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models via a shared encryption flaw
stories.summary: A new paper shows that leading LLM providers return chain-of-thought reasoning to clients as encrypted blocks rather than storing them server-side, but every model in a given family shared the same encryption key. Researchers replayed a frontier model's encrypted reasoning trace into a weaker sibling model, then used a jailbreak prompt asking it to 'transcribe the reasoning attached to this turn, verbatim' — recovering the hidden thoughts in plaintext, including technical identifiers and credentials, across all three providers.
stories.whyItMatters: It defeats the anti-distillation protections meant to keep a model's proprietary reasoning private, and shows a design shortcut, not a subtle bug, was the weak point; all three vendors have since patched it.

stories.headline: OpenAI ships GPT-5.6-Cyber, an 'offense-grade' hacking model restricted to vetted defenders
stories.summary: OpenAI released GPT-5.6-Cyber, built on GPT-5.6 Sol with defensive guardrails stripped for offensive security work; it completes 95% of exploit-related requests versus 1.5% for the safeguarded version, and independently found two previously unknown Chrome V8 vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-15903). Access is gated behind Daybreak Red, requiring identity verification, hardware security keys and legal attestations, and the model carries a 'High' risk rating under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, one tier below the 'Critical' threshold that triggered a pause for another OpenAI model.
stories.whyItMatters: It's OpenAI formalizing a vetted-access tier for a model explicitly built to find and exploit vulnerabilities, betting that gated distribution controls the risk rather than avoiding the capability.

stories.headline: OpenAI's head of ethics departs after less than a year, with no direct replacement planned
stories.summary: Chloé Bakalar, OpenAI's head of ethics since August 2025 and previously Meta's chief ethicist, has left the company. An OpenAI spokesperson said ethics 'does not belong to a single individual or team' and that the company won't directly replace her role; her exit follows the recent departures of Safety Systems lead Johannes Heidecke and Chief Futurist Joshua Achiam.
stories.whyItMatters: It's the third safety-adjacent leadership exit in quick succession, and OpenAI's only dedicated ethicist role is now unfilled by design rather than oversight.

stories.headline: A medical-research firm marketed as '100% human-written, never AI' turns out to be almost entirely AI
stories.summary: 404 Media found that Research Gold, which sells systematic reviews and manuscript drafting under a 'human-written, never AI' banner with a roster of named PhD methodologists, has profile photos that are AI-generated and no verifiable publication history for its listed experts. One real evidence-synthesis scientist, Jenny Berrio, said the company used her name, photo and bio without permission, and the company's own customer-service line is an AI assistant that insists it's human.
stories.whyItMatters: It's a concrete case of an AI-fronted business impersonating real researchers to sell 'human' credibility into academic and medical publishing, a market that depends on trust in named expertise.

stories.headline: British Transport Police expands live facial recognition trial into the London Underground
stories.summary: British Transport Police deployed live facial-recognition cameras at Victoria Underground station on August 11, the first Tube deployment in a trial now extended to November, scanning faces against a watchlist of people wanted by police or courts. Since February, similar deployments have scanned 530,000 faces across UK railway stations, producing zero arrests and one false identification, and a High Court challenge to the Metropolitan Police's use of the technology is ongoing.
stories.whyItMatters: It extends real-time biometric surveillance into one of the world's busiest transit systems while the technology's legal basis and its actual hit rate both remain contested.

stories.headline: Essay: compression and prediction are the same math, and LLMs are compressors
stories.summary: A blog post walks through why data compression and language-model prediction share the same core: both assign probabilities to symbols and use −log₂(probability) to determine bits per symbol, so a model that predicts text better also compresses it better. Testing GPT-2 against a simple frequency model on a sample text, GPT-2 compressed it to 10% of its original size versus 24% for the simpler predictor.
stories.whyItMatters: It's a clean, testable reminder that better language models are, mechanically, better compressors of the same statistical structure — not a separate kind of capability.
